# Benchmarks

<!-- Generated by `npm run stress`; profile sections are replaced on each run. Edit the notes at the end freely. -->

Measured on **2026-11-15** on one machine running everything: the API server, MongoDB, the load generator and
every dashboard client.

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 7445HS w/ Radeon 740M Graphics (12 threads) |
| Memory | 15 GB |
| OS | Linux 7.0.0-43-generic |
| Node.js | v22.23.4 |
| MongoDB | 7.0.48 (local, Docker) |

**How it works.** `tools/stress` registers its own ingest agents and sends events through the real
`POST /api/v1/ingest` path (agent key, token bucket, load shedding, validation, dedup, aggregation, bulk writes),
using the simulator's agent code, so batches, 429 back-off and thinning behave as in production. It opens
the requested number of Socket.IO dashboard clients; each joins its fleet rooms, `meta` and three random
`node:` rooms, like a user on the Overview with three node pages open. The server's own numbers come from
`GET /api/v1/meta/stats` once a second.

**Reading the latencies.** *Socket delivery* is the time from the server emitting `meta:pt` to a client
receiving it (same machine, so no clock skew). *Ingest → client* starts at the beginning of a point's
1-second bucket, so it includes the bucket itself (up to 1 s) and the aggregator's 2 s grace period for late
events, by design; the rest is processing and delivery.

<!-- stress:notes -->
## What the numbers say

| Profile | Offered | Accepted | Clients | Socket delivery p95 | Worst loop lag p99 | Shedding |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| [Baseline](#baseline-the-demo-fleet): 48 nodes × 2 Hz | 96 /s | 96 /s | 10 | 1 ms | 15 ms | none |
| [Heavy](#heavy-10-the-nodes-25-the-rate-200-dashboards): 500 nodes × 5 Hz | 2,500 /s | 2,500 /s | 200 | 13 ms | 26 ms | none |
| [High](#high-10000-eventss-to-200-dashboards): 2,000 nodes × 5 Hz | 10,000 /s | 9,989 /s | 200 | 27 ms | 27 ms | none |
| [Max](#max-50000-eventss-from-10000-nodes): 10,000 nodes × 5 Hz | 50,000 /s | 37,984 /s | 50 | 33 ms | 127 ms | 14 of 90 s, off 3 s after the load dropped |

- **Up to 10,000 events/s to 200 dashboards there is no strain at all**: every event accepted, no 429, socket
  delivery under 30 ms at p95, event-loop lag under 30 ms, and the write buffer empty at every sample.
  The demo fleet uses about 1% of that.
- **Delivery stays fast under load.** Even at 50,000 events/s, a dashboard receives the server's emits in
  33 ms at p95. Ingest → client is about 3.1 s at every load level: that is the 1-second bucket plus the
  aggregator's deliberate 2-second wait for late events, not queueing.
- **At 50,000 events/s from 10,000 nodes, backpressure does its job.** A single Node.js process with a
  1.4 GB heap spends long enough in garbage collection that event-loop lag passes the 150 ms threshold in
  short bursts. Ingest then answers 429 with `Retry-After`, agents pause, lag falls, shedding switches off;
  76% of the offered load is accepted, dashboards keep receiving, and shedding stops for good 3 s after the
  load drops. Agents only buffer 2,000 events each, so about 1 million events were discarded at the
  source while they waited — the intended trade: fresh data over a backlog.
- **Rate is cheap; nodes are what cost.** 2,000 nodes at 15 Hz (30,000 events/s) ran clean, while memory
  and write volume grow with the number of nodes, because the aggregator turns any number of events per node
  into one point per second and keeps each node's last 60 s of buckets in memory so late events can still
  correct them.

### Where it breaks

- **20,000 nodes × 5 Hz (100,000 events/s): the server runs out of memory.** Shedding switched on, but
  shedding cuts events, not nodes, and the 60 s of per-node buckets passed Node's default 2 GB heap about
  20 s into the run (`FATAL ERROR: … JavaScript heap out of memory`). That is the ceiling of one process
  with these settings; going past it means a larger heap, a shorter late-event window, or several ingest
  processes, each owning part of the fleet.

### A bottleneck found and fixed

The first runs broke at only **4,000 nodes × 2.5 Hz** (10,000 events/s): 12 s of shedding, about 16% of
events accepted, the write buffer at 90%. MongoDB was not the limit — it wrote 1,000 points in about 80 ms.
The writer was: it flushes at most 1,000 points at a time, and after a flush it waited for the next point
to arrive before flushing again. Points arrive in bursts every 250 ms when buckets close, so it drained
about 4,000 points/s, one per node per second. It now drains a backlog flush after flush
(`server/src/pipeline/writer.ts`, with a test in `writer.test.ts`):

| Probe (20 s, 50 clients) | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 4,000 nodes × 2.5 Hz (10,000 events/s) | 16% accepted, 12 s shedding, loop lag up to 1.9 s | 100% accepted, no shedding, loop lag ≤ 22 ms |
| 5,000 nodes × 5 Hz (25,000 events/s) | 17% accepted, 14 s shedding | 100% accepted, 1 s of shedding while 5,000 new nodes registered |

### Caveats

- One laptop runs the server, MongoDB, the load generator and every client, so they compete for CPU; a
  separate load machine would show the server in a better light, not a worse one.
- The hosted API runs on Render's free instance (a fraction of one CPU). Its event-loop lag sits near the
  150 ms threshold even at the demo's 96 events/s, so the Pipeline page there shows brief shedding blips and
  about 3% of batches are retried. These benchmarks are local; the hosted numbers are not comparable.
- Each profile ran on a fresh server and an empty database (`epicenter_stress`), with the simulator off.

### Reproduce

```bash
MONGODB_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/epicenter_stress npm run seed
MONGODB_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/epicenter_stress PORT=4300 NODE_ENV=production npm run start -w @epicenter/server
# in another terminal; a fresh server per profile keeps earlier stress nodes from going silent mid-run
npm run stress -- --url http://localhost:4300 --mongo mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/epicenter_stress --profile baseline
```

Profiles: `baseline`, `heavy`, `high`, `max`, `all`, or custom (`--nodes --hz --clients --duration`). The
tool refuses non-local URLs and Atlas connection strings unless `--allow-remote`, because stress nodes are
registered permanently.
